I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me..."﴾ [Ibrahim: 22].

That is, I had no authority of proof that could convince you, nor any authority of force and power that could terrify you and compel you into disobedience. Rather, you were at a mere (tashwira), a simple signal: as soon as I called you, you responded. ﴿So do not blame me, but blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me...﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. We say: "So-and-so cried out, and I answered his cry," meaning: I removed the causes of his crying out.

As for His words: ﴿to Pharaoh, Haman, and Qarun...﴾ [Ghafir: 24]: Pharaoh was indeed the head of the trial and the claimant to divinity, but Haman is mentioned with him because he was his minister and assistant, and Qarun because he was in charge of his treasury. So the three were partners, and therefore they also shared in accusing Musa: ﴿they said, "A sorcerer, a liar."﴾ [Ghafir: 24].

﴿So when he brought them the truth from Us...﴾ [Ghafir: 25], meaning: the signs. ﴿they said, "Kill the sons of those who believe with him..."﴾ [Ghafir: 25]. The matter of killing the sons came from Pharaoh twice. The first was in the days when Musa was a child. Pharaoh learned from the astrologers that his rule would end at the hands of one of the sons of the Children of Israel, so he began killing the young boys, out of fear of this child who would be born and at whose hands his kingdom would fall.

What is remarkable here is the stupidity and heedlessness of Pharaoh in killing the sons of the Children of Israel, and his eagerness that not one of them should escape, to the point that his men would enter the houses searching them for young children.

This situation revealed his stupidity in two respects. First: he kills the young sons, although the prophecy says that the end of his rule would come at the hands of one of them. Then a boy comes to him in this suspicious manner: a chest in the sea, with a young boy inside, arriving at the door of his house. He feels reassured by him, takes him, raises him under his own eye, and remains heedless of what is intended for him.

This situation is clarified by His words: ﴿And know that Allah comes between a person and his heart...﴾ [Al-Anfal: 24]. Indeed, the hearts are between two fingers of the All-Merciful; He turns them however He wills.

As for His words ﴿and spare their women...﴾ [Ghafir: 25], meaning: kill the male sons, because they are the source of fear, from them comes rebellion, and from them will come the one at whose hands Pharaoh's kingdom will fall. As for the women, leave them alive for service and for humiliation.

This explains to us why the Arabs, when they went out to war, took their women with them, so that they would share one fate with them: if they were victorious, they would return safe, and if they were killed, they would all be killed together, so that no women would remain after them to be taken captive, enslaved, and humiliated.

﴿And the scheming of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾ [Ghafir: 25]. Indeed, this was a scheme from Pharaoh and his helpers. But did his scheme succeed against the Children of Israel? No; rather, Allah turned his scheme back upon him, and he returned with error and loss.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 40, verse 26:

Pharaoh's saying "Leave me, let me kill Moses" (ذَرُونِيۤ أَقْتُلْ مُوسَىٰ): meaning, leave me to kill him. This indicates the presence of a group among the people who prevented Pharaoh from killing Moses; otherwise he would not have said "leave me." Who were these people? Perhaps they were among Pharaoh's followers who truly believed in Moses and in what he brought, so they wished to defend him in a way that would not arouse Pharaoh's suspicion, and so they devised a stratagem against him.

This is evidence that people of goodness may employ stratagems against people of evil to support what is good, and that God helps them. These people came and said to Pharaoh: "If you kill Moses, the people will say that he is upon the truth, and that you were unable to refute his proof, so you killed him to be rid of him, and then they will stand against you."

Among these defenders of Moses was the believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who was concealing his faith out of fear of Pharaoh's oppression, and who defended Moses with strong argument and presented proofs, saying: ﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾ [Ghafir: 28].

Consider here Pharaoh's mockery and derision in ﴿and let him call upon his Lord﴾: that is, his Lord to whom he calls, that He may rescue him. Had he not been mocking, he would have said: ﴿Let him call upon our Lord; indeed, I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾. Glory be to God, see how the people of falsehood try to invert realities: Pharaoh feared that Moses would change the religion of his people, while their religion was belief in Pharaoh as a god they worship besides God.

As for ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾: from where does corruption arise? From the existence of two groups in society: a group that believes in Pharaoh as a god, and a group that believes in Moses and his true Lord. The entire populace is then in discord and strife, and those in positions of power who profit from Pharaoh's divinity will not remain silent. There is no doubt that this is a sedition which, in his view, will produce corruption.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 40, verse 27:

Here Musa affirms the lordship (rububiyyah) of the Truth, glory be to Him, after Pharaoh threatened him with death: ﴿Leave me to kill Musa﴾. Then Pharaoh mocked his Lord: ﴿And let him call upon his Lord﴾. Therefore Musa's reply begins with ﴿Indeed I⦆ (inni), which contains an affirmation and a reminder of his own servitude before the might of the lordship that Pharaoh mocks. Had he simply said, "I seek refuge in Allah from your deed," he would have affirmed that Allah is his Lord, but ﴿and your Lord﴾ as well.

The meaning of ʿudhtu is: I took refuge in Him, and He is capable of giving me victory and protection. So his words ﴿Indeed I have taken refuge in my Lord﴾ show us the rank of seeking refuge in Allah. When a person seeks refuge in Allah from something he cannot withstand, he has truly submitted and been fair, because he has placed against the one who harmed him one who is able to do what he himself cannot: to turn him back.

Here Musa, peace be upon him, says: "Indeed I seek refuge in Allah from you, O Pharaoh, and He is stronger than you and capable of protecting me from your plotting. He is (my Lord), that is, the One who created me and nurtured me, and I am accountable to Him. He brought me into existence by His power and preserves me by His self-subsistence. Do you not see that every maker guards his creation and provides a guarantee for its preservation?

Is the Creator, glory be to Him, not more worthy to guarantee for me the life He created? Indeed, on the condition that you say it: ﴿I have taken refuge in my Lord﴾.

It would have sufficed for him to say "Indeed I have taken refuge in my Lord," so why did he add ﴿and your Lord﴾? They said: to affirm the lordship of his Lord, mighty and majestic, and to affirm his happiness through this lordship. He is my Lord, and the Lord of the others and of you all, so that they may say it along with him: "Indeed we have taken refuge in our Lord from Pharaoh and his deeds." It is as if he wishes to gather the forces of goodness and faith and strengthen his side with the believing community, so that the supplication is more likely to be accepted and more fitting.

This matter explains to us the importance of the community and the spirit of community in Islam. For instance, in the prayer we recite the Opening of the Book and say: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5], in the plural. Why did one not say: "You I worship and You I ask for help"? Because the supplication of the community is stronger. The community brings you into the company of the righteous; if you are not righteous, then associate with the righteous, perhaps what reaches them of reward and acceptance will reach you.

Therefore beware of despising the people of piety and the people of righteousness, for perhaps you will be taken up with them in pure grace...

From what did the master Musa seek refuge? ﴿From every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning﴾, in the plural form and with the description ﴿from every arrogant one﴾. He did not name his adversary Pharaoh, the party to the dispute, the claimant to divinity, and the one who threatened him with death. Why?

They said: Pharaoh was not mentioned in this position for two reasons.

First: so that Pharaoh would not be placed on a par with Allah, had he said, "I take refuge in my Lord from Pharaoh." Moreover, Pharaoh was not alone; there were others with him of his kind, so he wanted to include them all in a word that encompasses every arrogant one.

The second reason: the master Musa here observes the right of upbringing and preserves for Pharaoh this favour, so he did not name him explicitly, and it is enough that he is included in this description: ﴿from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning﴾...

As for His saying ﴿from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning﴾, it means that two qualities of evil were combined in him: he is arrogant, meaning hard-hearted, and hardness of heart does not restrain him from oppression and tyranny. Furthermore, he does not believe in the Reckoning, so he does not fear retribution and takes no account of consequences, and for such a person there is no hope of reform.

When Moses, peace be upon him, came to his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, and said: "Indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord," Allah responded to him and granted him protection, not through a messenger, nor an angel, nor any of his believing followers, but through a believing man from the family of Pharaoh who was concealing his faith out of fear of Pharaoh's brutality. He rose up in defense of Moses, and this is clearer in argument and more eloquent.

But why would he conceal his faith, if he was a believer? They said: they were wrapping their faith and hiding it, because they did not have the power by which they could repel tyranny. Faith resides in the soul until it finds the opportunity, then it appears and is openly proclaimed. And here it appears on the tongue of this believing man, who declares before Pharaoh and his tyranny that he is a believer, and calls to a call that is most similar to the call of the messengers, and informs of a method as if he were a messenger.

The phrase "yaktumu imanahu" (he concealed his faith) has in Islam a particular significance and history. The meaning of concealing faith is that faith tries to manifest in a man's conduct, but he conceals his faith. He is keen to make his faith a secret between himself and his Lord alone, so that he may speak the word of truth and proclaim it before the people while appearing not to be a believer, so that he is not harmed.

Thus: faith is an emotional act that matures across all the faculties of the human soul. The believer is found to be humble, submissive, who responds to the truth and yields to it. The believer is compassionate, generous, forbearing, merciful; you perceive his faith from his conduct, but he tries to conceal this until he stands in the position that enables him to proclaim Islam openly, strongly and forcefully.

Therefore they say: faith is an inner process of the heart, and it is a secret between the servant and his Lord; then it also has an outward aspect between the believer and people. The secret and the open may be intertwined, between him and his Lord and between him and the people. He may be a believer between himself and Allah, while between himself and the people he is either a believer or not a believer, because in the process of faith, he manifests more than what his faith displays...

But what did the believing man say?

He said: "Will you kill a man merely because he says, 'My Lord is Allah'?" Consider the boldness of truth in this believer: he declares with this rejecting question, "Will you kill a man," before Pharaoh, "merely because he says, 'My Lord is Allah'"; i.e., because of his saying "My Lord is Allah," with no offense other than this. The believing man says it openly before Pharaoh. And what do you know of Pharaoh? He is the one who claimed divinity and said to his people, "I know of no god for you other than myself" [al-Qasas: 38]. There is no doubt that the word of the believing man enraged him and demolished the pillars of his claimed divinity.

And his saying: "And he has certainly brought you clear proofs from your Lord," i.e., clear signs. So how can he be killed? And let us suppose he is a liar: his lie will not harm you, for he lied against Allah and will bear the consequence of this lie: "If he is a liar, then upon him is his lie; and if he is truthful, some of what he threatens you with will befall you" — meaning: if he was truthful, you would not be deprived of his good, and some of that good would reach you. So why would you kill him? Caution dictates that he not be killed.

But does that mean we should leave every atheist to say whatever he likes and engage in matters of religion, and not prevent him, relying on "if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie"? They said: No, rather we must supply a phrase here: prevent him from speaking, but do not kill him. We often hear of the heretics who now engage in the religion of Allah, so what should we do? Shall we leave them and say: upon them is their lie?

No, rather we must confront them and prevent them from this nonsense, and restrain their hands, so that they do not cause harm to the religion of Allah. Likewise the believing man from the family of Pharaoh said, defending our master Moses, peace be upon him, as if he wished to preserve the proof of truth, perhaps there would be ears later that would support it.

Then the Exalted declares this truth: "Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar." This statement is considered an allusion and a disparagement of Pharaoh. Allah the Exalted does not leave anyone who lies against Him without exposing his lie, and why? Because concealing this lie would be considered deception in the method of heaven, and far be it from Allah, the Exalted, to do that. Therefore we see that whenever someone claims prophethood, his matter is exposed and people learn of his lie, because it is not proper that a liar should claim prophethood and that Allah should not show people his lie. This is implied in His saying, and in His promise: "Indeed, We shall surely help Our messengers and those who believe, in the life of this world" [Ghafir: 51], and in His saying: "And indeed, Our soldiers will certainly be the victorious" [al-Saffat: 173].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 40, verse 29:

His saying: ﴿O my people, yours is the kingdom today, dominant in the land﴾. This is the speech of the believing man advising his people. Yes, they have the kingdom, meaning the kingdom of Pharaoh, his tyranny, his might, and his claim to divinity... etc. And ﴿dominant in the land﴾ means: victorious and superior over others. But beware, for this is a temporary state that will not last for you. It is restricted: ﴿yours is the kingdom today﴾. It is as if he is saying to them: beware lest this kingdom slip from your hands.

Perhaps this man, that is Musa (peace be upon him), is truthful, and will gather around him followers and supporters and bring an end to this kingdom. So spare yourselves, even at the cost of the error you are upon, and do not enter into a confrontation whose outcome you do not know. ﴿Who will help us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us?﴾ No one, because the might of Allah and His retribution, in support of His messengers, is a might that cannot be repelled, and it will certainly destroy the opponent. So beware. In this way the believing man speaks with the logic of faith firmly rooted in his soul, and he is sincere toward his people, not deceiving them.

Here Pharaoh must react and try to seize control of affairs for his own benefit: ﴿Pharaoh said: I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct﴾. Note the logic of domination in ﴿I show you only what I see﴾ and the logic of deception in ﴿and I guide you only to the path of right conduct﴾.

But Pharaoh's reaction did not prevent the believing man from continuing his call, nor did it stop him from advising his people: ﴿And the one who believed said: O my people, I fear for you...﴾

Here the believing man continues his counsel to his people. The word of Pharaoh did not frighten him, nor did it deter him from his call. So he says: ﴿O my people, I fear for you a day like the day of the factions﴾. That is, if you are dominant now on earth and have the upper hand, you are no more dominant than those who came before you in the procession of messages, from Noah onward, and ʿĀd, Thamūd, and those after them: ﴿like the habit of the people of Noah, and ʿĀd, and Thamūd, and those after them. And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants﴾.

Allah has shown us the wonder concerning those who denied the messengers: ﴿So each We seized for his sin. Among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of pebbles, and among them were those seized by the Cry, and among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them were those whom We drowned. And Allah would never wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 40].

So, you must take warning from those who came before you in denial, especially since you witness their traces on the earth, which show that they were stronger than you and had more monuments on the earth. Yet their strength did not benefit them, and their monuments did not protect them from the might of Allah when it descended upon them. Allah has left these traces only to serve as a lesson for those who come after them: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning, and at night. Will you not then reason?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 137-138].

Had their traces been effaced, there would be no conclusive proof. The survival of the traces until now shows us that those who built these civilizations and left these monuments could not protect their civilizations, though they were stronger than you in might and monuments on the earth, and they cultivated it more than you did. Since this has happened in reality and you witness it, take it as a word from the Messenger and as a reality before you in the cosmos.

We note here that the word (yawm, "day") came in the singular while (al-aḥzāb, "the factions") came in the plural. Why did he not say, for example, (ayyām al-aḥzāb, "days of the factions")? The ḥizb (faction) is the group opposing and denying the Messenger: one faction opposed Noah, another opposed Hūd, another Ṣāliḥ, and so on.

So the days here are many, yet he said: ﴿like the day of the factions﴾, making "day" singular and "factions" plural. Why? Because the event is as if it were one single occurrence unified across all of them. Although the factions multiplied with the multiplicity of messengers, it is "the day of the factions" and not "the days of the factions," because if we said "days of the factions," each would have its own cause, and another its own cause, and so on. But it is one cause in every case, namely denial in the matter of belief and in the matter of Allah's legislating the truth for creation, glory be to Him.

Then after that, what the word "al-Ahzab" summarized is explained in detail: ﴿Like the custom of the people of Noah, and 'Ad, and Thamud, and those after them. And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants.﴾ That is: He did not seize them with this seizure as an injustice to them. As for the phrase ﴿for the servants﴾, it means: how could He wrong them when they are His servants and His handiwork? Rather, He seized them as recompense for their deeds and their denial of His messengers, so that they would be a real lesson in the universe, by which everyone who opposes the method of truth would take heed.

The Day of Confrontation (yawm al-ahzab) was in this world, while the Day of Mutual Calling (yawm al-tanad) is the Day of Resurrection. It is as if he warned them, through the Day of the Confederates, of the calamities that would come upon them in their worldly lives, and then warned them of the Day of Recompense, the Day of Resurrection, saying: ﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Mutual Calling﴾.

Al-tanad is a reciprocal form (tafa'ul), meaning: you call out to me and I call out to you. The mutual calling on the Day of Resurrection will take place in several ways. The Exalted says: ﴿The Day We will call every people with their leader﴾ [al-Isra': 71]. This is the first calling: one says, "O community of Muhammad, O community of Jesus, O community of Moses," and so on. Or some of them call out to others.

The Exalted has mentioned various images of these callings. He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire, "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true. Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 44].

He said: ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden, "Pour upon us some water, or of what Allah has provided you..."﴾ [al-A'raf: 50].

And He said: ﴿And the companions of the Heights will call out to men whom they recognize by their marks...﴾ [al-A'raf: 48]. The companions of the Heights are a group whose good deeds and bad deeds were equal and who did not enter the Garden, yet they gloat over the disbelievers.

Or: the tanad is not from one of us calling to another, but rather from the verb (nadda), meaning: to be far away and to flee. That is, the Day of Tanad is the day when I flee from you and you flee from me. This is like the Exalted's saying: ﴿On the Day a man will flee from his brother, and his mother and his father, and his spouse and his children﴾ [Abasa: 34-36]. The meaning is that he flees from them, and they likewise flee from him, each fleeing from the other because he is preoccupied with himself.

But what does the believing man intend by this? They said: he wants to say to them: if you were supporting one another in falsehood in this world, know that you will flee from one another in the Hereafter, ﴿the Day you turn back fleeing﴾.

Reflect here on the artistry of the Qur'anic expression: when it uses a word that carries two meanings, or combines two meanings, it brings in what indicates each of them. Here, for example, He said ﴿yawm al-tanad﴾, in the sense of mutual calling (al-munadah).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 40, verse 33:

The Day of the Confederates (Yawm al-Ahzab) was in this world, whereas the Day of Mutual Calling (Yawm al-Tanad) is the Day of Resurrection. It is as if he warned them, by the Day of the Confederates, of the calamities that would come upon them in their worldly life, and then warned them of the Day of Recompense, the Day of Resurrection, saying: ﴿And O my people, I fear for you the Day of Mutual Calling﴾ [Ghafir: 32]. Tanad is on the pattern of tafa'ul (reciprocal action), meaning: you call me and I call you. The mutual calling on the Day of Resurrection will take several forms. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿The Day We shall summon every people with their leader﴾ [al-Isra: 71]. This is the first calling: he says, "O community of Muhammad, O community of Jesus, O community of Moses..." etc. Or it may be that some of them call out to one another.

The Glorified and Exalted has mentioned several forms of these callings. He, glorified be He, says: ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire, "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised to be true?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 44].

And He says: ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden, "Pour upon us some water, or some of what Allah has provided you..."﴾ [al-A'raf: 50].

And He says: ﴿And the companions of the Heights will call out to men whom they recognize by their marks...﴾ [al-A'raf: 48]. The companions of the Heights (Ashab al-A'raf) are a group whose good deeds and bad deeds were balanced and who did not enter the Garden; yet they gloat over the disbelievers.

Or: the tanad is not the calling of some of us to others, but rather derives from the verb (nadda), meaning: to be far away and to flee. That is, the Day of Mutual Calling is a day on which you flee from me and I flee from you. This is like His saying: ﴿The Day a man will flee from his brother, and his mother and his father, and his spouse and his children﴾ [Abasa: 34–36]. The meaning is: he flees from them, and they likewise flee from him, each fleeing the other because he is occupied with himself.

But what does the believing man intend by this? They say: he wants to say to them, "If you collude with one another in falsehood in this world, know that you will flee from one another in the Hereafter: ﴿The Day you turn back fleeing﴾ [Ghafir: 33].

Consider here the artistry of the Qur'anic expression: when it employs a word carrying two meanings, or combining two meanings, it brings forth what indicates each of them. Here, for example, He said ﴿the Day of Mutual Calling﴾ [Ghafir: 32], meaning calling out, and He said ﴿the Day you turn back fleeing﴾ [Ghafir: 33], meaning fleeing, so He combined both meanings in the one word (tanad).

Similarly, His saying in Surah al-Rahman: ﴿The sun and the moon [follow] a calculation, and the star and the tree prostrate﴾ [al-Rahman: 6]. The sun and the moon are celestial creatures, and the tree is earthly, and between them is the word (al-najm), which has two meanings. The first, which comes first to mind, is the star high in the sky, of the same kind as the sun and the moon. The other (najm) means: the herb that has no stem, which is of the genus of plants.

And His saying: ﴿You have no protector from Allah; and whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide﴾ [Ghafir: 33]. "No protector (min 'asim)" means: no one can prevent you from Allah, nor avert from you any calamity if it befalls you. ﴿And whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide﴾ means: whomever Allah decrees to be astray, no one can guide. Why? They say: because Allah, the Exalted, will assist him and enable him to go astray.

Therefore we have said: when a servant loves something, Allah says to His servant, "You loved it, O My servant, so I will try you with it." For example, a man whose beloved died grieves for him intensely, exaggerates in it, and persists in sorrow; then God says to him, "You loved grief and became infatuated with it; I will increase it for you, and whenever it ages, I will renew it for you."

Therefore the people of knowledge (ahl al-ma'rifa) said: close the doors of grief with the nails of contentment, for if you grow accustomed to grief and love it, Allah will perpetuate it for you, since He, glorified be He, is your Lord and the one who manages your affairs, and He gives each of you his desire. Even the disbeliever who loved disbelief, Allah has promised to help him in it; therefore He seals his heart so that faith cannot enter it and disbelief cannot leave it.

Then the believing man from the family of Pharaoh continues his admonition to his people, saying:

﴿And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs...﴾.

The Qur'anic verse references in the text are rendered as given in the commentary, and the passage is translated below.

When Yusuf (peace be upon him) came, there was no Pharaoh over Egypt in his time. Rather, there was a king, the ʿAzīz, and therefore when you read the story of our master Yusuf (peace be upon him), you find no mention of Pharaoh at all, as in the story of our master Musa. When we came to know the successive events of history and were able to return the events to their times, we learned that Yusuf was in the period of the shepherd kings (the Hyksos). These people, after they entered Egypt, put an end to the rule of the Pharaohs, abolished the Pharaonic system, and made themselves kings. Therefore the story says ﴿And the king said﴾ [Yusuf: 43], and did not say Pharaoh.

When Pharaonic rule returned once more, they began to persecute the Children of Israel, because they had been supporting the king and backing him.

His saying ﴿with clear proofs﴾ [Ghafir: 34] means: the clear signs that indicate his truthfulness in conveying the message from God. ﴿So you continued in doubt about what he had brought to you﴾ [Ghafir: 34] means: you were doubting the truth of his message. ﴿Until, when he perished﴾ [Ghafir: 34] means: died. ﴿You said, "God will never send after him any messenger"﴾ [Ghafir: 34]. They said this because they denied the message; they were hypocrites within themselves. ﴿Thus God leaves astray whoever is a transgressor﴾ [Ghafir: 34] means: one who exceeds the limit, ﴿a doubter﴾ [Ghafir: 34], one who is skeptical about the message and denies it.

Is there any argument concerning Allah that has authority to support it? They said: Yes. The argument intended is an argument concerning Allah, meaning concerning the command of Allah, for affirmation, and an argument from the opposing side to deny it. We have said that the signs (ayat) come in three meanings: cosmic signs that indicate the all-encompassing power of the Creator, glorified be He; signs that establish the truthfulness of the messengers in conveying from Allah, which are the miracles (mu'jizat); and the verses of the Qur'an that carry the rulings (ahkam). In which of these types were they arguing?

Firstly, they argued against the signs of the miracles and said of them that they were sorcery. The response to this claim is easy, for we say to them: The one who bewitched the people so that they believed in him, why did he not bewitch you too, so that you would believe in him? At that point the matter ends.

Likewise they argued against the verses of rulings. Why? Because every ruling that Allah sends down to His servants prevents the tyranny of one generation over another or of one individual over another, and this runs counter to the interests of those who hold power and pride on earth: ﴿That is the Last Abode. We assign it to those who do not desire haughtiness in the earth or corruption, and the final outcome is for the righteous﴾ [al-Qasas: 83].

As for the cosmic signs that establish the power of the Creator, glorified be He, such as the sun, the moon, the stars and others, they are not a field for argument, so they did not argue concerning them.

The meaning of ﴿It is greatly hateful﴾: that this argument concerning the signs of Allah without any right is an argument that is detestable, which Allah hates with great hatred, and which those who believe also hate, those who are keen on the religion of Allah and on strengthening the motives of faith in Him within souls.

﴿Thus does Allah seal every heart of an arrogant, tyrannical one﴾. The meaning of yatba'u (seals) is: He sets a seal upon his heart. The mutakabbir (arrogant one) is the one who feigns pride and claims it while he has no justification for it, so he is arrogant without any real basis for pride... So: we have said that the arrogant one is one who acts proudly while having no justification for pride. What if he had justifications for pride? We say: if he has justifications for pride, then his shortcoming is that he is proud of something that is not intrinsic to him and that may be taken from him, like one who is proud of his health, which Allah may take from him, because it is an accident that passes away from you. Furthermore, when the arrogant one sees one greater than himself, his pride diminishes; and if he had seen with his inner insight the greatness of his Lord, he would never have been arrogant.

Pharaoh commands his minister and aide Haman to build him a lofty tower that he may ascend upon, so that perhaps he may see this god whom Moses calls him to worship, as if the tower would bring him to the sight of God. But God, the God you would see from a tower, cannot be a god. ﴿And thus was the evil of his deeds made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was barred from the path; and the scheming of Pharaoh was nothing but in ruin﴾ [Ghafir: 37]. That is: misguidance and loss. He will not remain thus; rather he will rise and keep rising until God exposes his affair on the day of drowning.

Pharaoh commands his minister and aide Haman to build him a lofty tower that he may ascend upon, so that perhaps he may see this god whom Moses calls him to worship, as if the tower would bring him to the sight of God. But God, the God you would see from a tower, cannot be a god. ﴿And thus was the evil of his deeds made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was barred from the path; and the scheming of Pharaoh was nothing but in ruin﴾ [Ghafir: 37]. That is: misguidance and loss. He will not remain thus; rather he will rise and keep rising until God exposes his affair on the day of drowning.

This is the saying of the believing man from Pharaoh's family, admonishing his people as though he were a prophet. If you ask: what silenced him from Pharaoh, so that Pharaoh, in his misguidance, reached the point of claiming divinity? They said: this is among our statements that truth has a charge (ṣawlah), but it has its appropriate time. And at the moment truth speaks on the tongue of this believer, it is as though the Truthful One (subḥānahu) Himself is speaking. Therefore no one opposed him, because the inspiration of the Most Merciful (wārid al-Raḥmān) is not opposed; what is opposed is the inspiration of humans (wārid al-bashar).

Thus, when the Truthful One said: ﴿And We inspired to the mother of Moses: Suckle him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear and do not grieve﴾ [al-Qasas: 7], she did not oppose this opinion. Who would say to a woman: if she fears for her infant, throw him into the river? By God, if anyone other than the Truthful One had said it, it would have been opposed. But Moses' mother accepted it and did not object, because the inspiration of the Most Merciful is not opposed and is not debated; otherwise she could have said: Shall I save him from a probable death to a certain death?

So there is no wonder that the believing man says these words in the sight and hearing of Pharaoh, and yet he did not oppose him.

﴿O my people, this worldly life is only enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement﴾ [Ghafir: 39]. This turns our attention to the fact that a person, in the events of life, must serve an aim (ghāyah), and a condition of the aim that serves is that there be no further aim after it. If there is another aim after it, then it is not an aim, but rather a stage leading to the aim. Like a child you educate so that he may obtain the preparatory certificate (al-i'dādiyyah), for example: is the preparatory certificate an aim? No, it is a stage leading to another stage, the secondary (al-thānawiyyah); likewise the secondary is a stage leading to what comes after it. So whatever has an "after" is not an aim; the aim is that which has no "after." Therefore the believing man tells them: the whole world, with all that is in it, is merely enjoyment, not an aim; the true aim is the Hereafter.

A reflective view sees that a person has an estimated lifespan in the cosmos that is not specified; God left it vague, and this vagueness is itself the clearest explanation and its highest degree. For when He made it vague in time and in place, He made us expect it and await it at every moment and in every place. Therefore they said: death is an arrow sent toward you, and it is already on its way to you, and your life is by the measure of its journey to you.

When you contemplate the cosmos around you, you find that the Creator has created for you a harmonious cosmos that serves you: sun, moon, stars, air, water, plants, and so on. So consider, O you for whom these worlds were created: how you perish while they remain! You die while the sun is as it is, and the moon, the stars, the air and the water; nothing in God's cosmos has changed. Even the water that we think diminishes has remained in the cosmos as it has been since God created it; it neither increases nor decreases.

The water you took from the cosmos during your life leaves you again in the form of sweat and waste; even the proportion that remains in us after death comes out and the earth absorbs it; likewise the water in a rose, for example, and in all living beings. So the whole cosmos is, likewise, a set of changes within a single unity.

But is it reasonable that the servant should live longer than the one served? I die while the sun that serves me, which was created for my sake, remains? Yes, so that you know that your servant lives longer than you in this world, though you are the honored one who is served. Therefore there must be for me another life that befits this honor: a life that remains after these creatures perish, when the sun, the moon and the stars come to an end, and I remain. This can only be in the Hereafter: ﴿On the day when the earth will be changed to another earth, and the heavens as well, and they will come forth before God, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Ibrahim: 48].

The believer must affirm this Day and believe in it, so that he may truly be the honored one and the one with the longer life. Even death itself dies, and you remain in the Hereafter, eternal; the blessing does not escape you and death does not overtake you.

Therefore the Truthful One wants us to look toward this aim, not to look beneath our feet, and to live only for the moment we are in. The true aim of every believer is the Hereafter, because it has no "after": ﴿And indeed the Abode of the Hereafter, that is the true life, if they only knew﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 64]; and al-hayawān is an intensive form of al-ḥayāh (life), i.e., the true life.

And here the believing man says: ﴿O my people, this worldly life is only enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement﴾ [Ghafir: 39], i.e., the place of permanent residence from which there is no departure and no other dwelling, and for which we must indeed work.

O my people, this worldly life is only an enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement. (Qur'an 40:39)

This makes us turn our attention to the fact that a human being, in the events of life, must necessarily be serving some end. A condition of the end that one serves is that there should be no further end beyond it. If there is another end after it, then it is not an end, but rather a stage leading to the end. Take, for example, a child whom you educate so that he may obtain the preparatory certificate. Is the preparatory certificate an end? No. It is only a stage leading to another stage, which is secondary school. Likewise, secondary school is a stage leading to what comes after it. So a thing, as long as there is something after it, is not an end; the end is that which has nothing after it. Therefore the believing man says to them: indeed the whole of this world, with everything in it, is merely enjoyment, not an end; the true end is the Hereafter.

Reflection shows that a human being has a presumed lifespan in the cosmos, not specified, which God left undetermined. This indefiniteness is itself the clearest explanation and its highest degree, because when He, glorified is He, left it undetermined in time and in place, He made us expect it and await it at every moment and in every place. That is why they said: death is an arrow that has been shot at you; it is already on its way toward you, and your lifespan is measured by the length of its journey to you.

The water you took from the universe during your life leaves you again in the form of sweat and waste, and even the portion that remains in us after death comes out and is absorbed by the earth. Likewise the water in a rose, for example, and in all living things. Thus the whole universe is a set of changes within a single unity.

But is it reasonable that the servant should live longer than the one served? I die, and the sun that serves me remains, the sun that was created for my sake? Yes, so that you know that your servant lives longer than you in this world, although you are the honored one who is served. Therefore, there must be for me another life that befits this honor, a life that remains after these creatures perish, when the sun, moon and stars come to an end, and I remain. This can only be in the Hereafter, the day when the earth will be replaced by another earth, and the heavens as well, and they will come forth before God, the One, the Subduer [Ibrahim: 48].

The believer must affirm this day and believe in it, so that he may truly be the honored one and the one with the longer life. Even death itself dies, and you remain in the Hereafter eternal; the blessing does not escape you and death does not overtake you.

Therefore the Truth, glorified is He, wants us to look toward this end, not to look at what is beneath our feet, and to live only for the moment we are in. The true end of every believer is the Hereafter, because it has nothing beyond it: "And indeed the Abode of the Hereafter, that is the true life, if they only knew" [al-Ankabut: 64]. Al-Hayawan is an intensive form of al-Hayat (life), meaning: the true life.

Here the believing man says: "O my people, this worldly life is only an enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement" [Ghafir: 39], meaning the permanent dwelling from which there is no departing, and no other residence, and we must work for it.

Yes, indeed. Since the Hereafter is the abode of settlement and permanence, there must be a return to Me and a standing before Me, and I will recompense each person according to his deeds. I am not a tyrant over you; rather, I am Merciful to you. I requite an evil deed with its like, or I forgive it, and I multiply a good deed many times over.

The pause here is at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and he is a believer﴾. This condition does not prevent non-believers from doing good and righteous deeds. The Truth, glory be to Him, has clarified this matter in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We increase for him in his tilth; and whoever desires the tilth of this world, We give him of it, but he has no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20].

When the disbeliever does good, he takes his portion of it in this world; he has no share in the reward of the Hereafter. He receives it in this world as fame, renown, and a good reputation on people's tongues; he receives it in the form of honor and celebration. Do you not see them erecting statues for them and immortalizing their memory... etc.

So: they have taken their portion in this world. Therefore, the Exalted says: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty one thinks to be water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and finds Allah with him, and He pays him his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ [al-Nur: 39].

Reflect on ﴿and found Allah with him﴾ [al-Nur: 39]. It means: he is confronted with it (his deed), because it was never in his mind in this world, nor did he ever do it for His sake. And it is well known that a person takes his wage from the one for whom he worked.

We were asked about this matter in San Francisco: Is the reward of a disbeliever who did good in this world lost? I said: Did he work for good for the sake of God, or for humanity and its advancement? They said: He worked for humanity, its advancement, and its service. I said: Then let him take his reward from it, for he has already taken it as fame, renown, and immortality. The Exalted says: ﴿And We will turn to the deeds they did, and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23].

Therefore we say: the disbelievers who worked for the advancement and progress of society, we benefit from their deeds, their inventions, and their discoveries, and we even adapt them to serve faith and the call to God. This recorder, this microphone, and others are the fruit of their effort. But they have no share in its reward. Therefore we say: these are servants of one letter of the letters of the Qur'an. What is it? It is the sin (س) in the Exalted's saying: ﴿We will show them Our signs on the horizons﴾ [Fussilat: 53].

They toil and live a harsh life of austerity in order to devote themselves to research and study, to reach one of God's secrets in His universe. In the end, people benefit from their works, while they themselves are deprived of the reward of this work.

As for His saying: ﴿Those will enter Paradise, being provided for therein without reckoning﴾. Provision (rizq) is everything by which a person benefits, not merely wealth as some suppose. Well-being is provision, safety is provision, knowledge is provision, and forbearance is provision. Everything by which you benefit is provision for you, "without reckoning." The word "reckoning" (hisab) means that you calculate a thing according to its measure.

As for the Hereafter, provision there is "without reckoning," that is, without reckoning by anyone, because the Giver and Provider is God. When God gives you, He does not give you according to your deeds; rather, He gives you according to His own measure, glory be to Him.

And when good comes to you unexpectedly, you say: "I did not count on it." So the meaning of "without reckoning" is: boundless power in giving, a power that gives to the giver without a calculated reckoning from him, and without a reckoning according to your measure. The matter, then, is vast.

This is the speech of the believing man from the family of Pharaoh; it is as if it were the speech of the prophets. I have not yet found a reason that satisfies me as to how Pharaoh kept silent about this speech. I can only say: God, glory be to Him, is able to combine a thing and its opposite. The believer proclaims this words of faith, but the Truth, glory be to Him, causes something else to enter the ear of Pharaoh; otherwise he would not have kept silent about it and left him to speak with this faith-based reasoning that demolishes Pharaoh's claimed divinity. Or, as we have said, the inspiration of the Most Merciful is not opposed.

As for His saying: ﴿مَا لِيۤ﴾ ("What is wrong with me?"), it is a question about something within himself: ﴿How do I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?﴾ That is, to what leads to salvation and what leads to the Fire. They said: because goodness is not goodness unless you love for others what you love for yourself. Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself."

This is the speech of the believing man from the family of Pharaoh; it is as if it were the speech of the prophets. Until now I have not been guided to a cause that satisfies me as to how Pharaoh remained silent over this speech. I can only say: Allah, glorified is He, is able to combine a thing and its opposite. The believer proclaims this word of faith openly, but the Truthful One (al-Haqq, subhanahu) causes something other than that to enter the ear of Pharaoh; otherwise he would not have stayed silent about it and let him speak with this faithful logic that demolishes Pharaoh's claimed divinity. Or, as we have said, the inspiration of the Most Merciful (warid al-Rahman) is not opposed.

And His saying: ﴿مَا لِيۤ﴾ [Ghafir: 41] ("What is with me?") is a question about something in himself: how can I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire? That is, to what leads to salvation and to what leads to the Fire. It has been said: goodness is not goodness unless you love for others what you love for yourself; therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said... Then he clarifies the meaning of ﴿أَدْعُوكُـمْ إِلَى ٱلنَّجَاةِ وَتَدْعُونَنِيۤ إِلَى ٱلنَّارِ﴾ [Ghafir: 41] ("I call you to salvation, and you call me to the Fire") by saying: ﴿تَدْعُونَنِي لأَكْـفُرَ بِٱللَّهِ وَأُشْرِكَ بِهِ مَا لَيْسَ لِي بِهِ عِلْمٌ وَأَنَاْ أَدْعُوكُمْ إِلَى ٱلْعَزِيزِ ٱلْغَفَّارِ﴾ [Ghafir: 42] ("You call me to disbelieve in Allah and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I call you to the All-Mighty, the Oft-Forgiving"). That is, you urge me to disbelieve in Allah and to associate partners with Him, while I urge you to believe in Him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 40, verse 43:

The word (lā jaram) means: without doubt and without question. ﴿Undoubtedly what you call me to﴾ means: to worship other than Allah. ﴿has no call⁠—﴾ meaning: no answered supplication, because they do not hear the supplication, and even if they heard it, they would not respond. ﴿And that our return⁠—﴾ meaning: our going back and our destination, the final end of our journey, ﴿is to Allah. And that the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾ meaning: they deserve it and are fit for it, as though they were its inhabitants.

The meaning of ﴿the transgressors﴾ is: those who exceed the limit in disbelief and tyranny. The worst of them is the one who transgresses against himself, going beyond the limit at which he ought to stop, and this limit may be either in the commands or in the prohibitions.

Almighty Allah clarifies this matter for us in His saying: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], meaning in the commands. And He says regarding the prohibitions: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187].

So regarding the commands, be careful not to overstep them; and regarding the prohibitions, He does not say to you, "Do not do it," but rather, "Do not approach it," do not draw near to it nor to the means that lead to it, for whoever grazes around the protected pasture is about to fall into it. The believer must respect this precaution from his Lord, because He is his Creator and knows him better than he knows himself.

When the believing man concludes his admonition to his people with His saying ﴿And that the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir: 43], it is as though he wants to allude to Pharaoh, who reached the peak of transgression against himself. For the matter of transgression in religion is that you may not listen to the call of truth, you may neglect its commands and turn away from its prohibitions, you may even abandon belief in Allah altogether. But this tyrant went beyond all of this, for he claimed divinity himself and said to his people: ﴿So he said, "I am your lord, the Most High"﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24]. And what transgression could be greater than this?

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 40, verse 44:

His saying ﴿So you will remember what I say to you﴾ [Ghafir: 44] means: if you now deny me, while I wish to deliver you from the servitude to Pharaoh to which you have become accustomed, then you will remember what I have said to you of counsel. The meaning is that you will remember it either in this world or in the Hereafter. ﴿And I entrust my affair to Allah﴾ [Ghafir: 44], that is, I return my affair to Him, glorified is He, for He is my Protector (walî).

It is as if he sensed that these words he had spoken would anger Pharaoh, who would surely plot against him to take revenge without confrontation or open opposition, lest he rally the people against him. So he said, ﴿And I entrust my affair to Allah﴾ [Ghafir: 44]?

That is: if you have been afflicted with a matter as a result of what you have engaged in, namely explaining the way of Allah, defending His Messenger Musa, and listening to the true path and following it, then I hope that He will grant me of deeds what benefits me in the Hereafter. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of the servants﴾ [Ghafir: 44]. So the result of entrusting his affair to Allah was:

﴿So Allah protected him from the evils of what they plotted...﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 40, verses 45–46:

God's words: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾ [Ghafir: 45]. That is: no harm befell him. This is a matter that calls for wonder, for this man stands before whom? Before Pharaoh. Yet no harm reached him, and Pharaoh's attempts at vengeance against him did him no damage. But why wonder? Protection comes from God: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾ [Ghafir: 45], because the act is not judged in itself, nor taken in itself. Rather, the act is judged together with its doer; the act must be accompanied by the one who performs it. An act may be one and the same, yet its ruling differs, being a cause of happiness or of misery depending on the doer.

Let us suppose that your son came in to you with blood flowing from his face. What is the first question you would rush to ask him? Who did this to you? Thus you are not preoccupied with the blood flowing from him as much as you are preoccupied with who did this. If he said: "My uncle So-and-so hit me," you would calm down and say: "He must have done something deserving punishment, so he hit you." But if he said: "The son of So-and-so hit me," you would say: "Yes, because he hates us, and such-and-such." And you would turn the world upside down.

So every act is not judged in itself, but together with its doer, and your knowledge of the doer is what determines your reaction to the act.

This matter also resolved for us the difficulty concerning the Isra' and Mi'raj, and explained to us God's words: ﴿Glory be to the One who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. Since the one who made the night journey is God, there is no wonder, for the act befits its doer, and God is exalted above time, place, and everything resembling creation. Had it said: "Muhammad traveled by night," there would have been discussion and dispute. But since God made him travel, there is no wonder in it. It is like if you said: "I climbed with my infant son to the summit of the Himalayas." Would anyone say: "How did the infant climb to the summit of the Himalayas?"

The same holds here. When the protection comes from God, what power or what tyrant or oppressor could harm you, when God is your protector against him? This protection came as a response to the entrusting of the matter to God Most High. The believing man said: ﴿And I entrust my affair to God﴾ [Ghafir: 44], so the response came immediately: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾ [Ghafir: 45].

Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq stopped at this verse, drew from it some subtleties and wisdoms, and said:

I wonder at one who fears and does not turn to God's words: ﴿God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 173], for I heard God after it say: ﴿So they returned with a blessing from God and bounty, no harm touched them…﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 174].

I wonder at one who is plotted against and does not turn to God's words: ﴿And I entrust my affair to God﴾ [Ghafir: 44], for I heard God after it say: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾ [Ghafir: 45].

I wonder at one who seeks the world and its adornment and does not turn to God's words: ﴿What God wills [is so]; there is no power except through God﴾ [al-Kahf: 39], for I heard God after it say: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾ [al-Kahf: 40].

I wonder at one who is distressed (al-ightimam, which is the tightening of the chest and shortness of breath without your knowing its cause) and does not turn to God's words: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87], for I heard God after it say: ﴿So We responded to him and saved him from the distress, and thus We save the believers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 88]. That is: it is not specific to him alone.

These are among the subtleties and refinements of God's Book. Whoever takes them as a regular litany, nothing of this will pass him by, and God will save him and protect him from fear, from plotting, from poverty, and from distress.

Then, the response of the Truthful, glorified is He, to His believing servant did not stop at protecting him from his enemy, but extended to the enemy himself, where the situation reversed and the circle turned against him. Reflect: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted, and there befell the family of Pharaoh the worst of punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 45]. That is: there descended upon them and there settled upon them the worst of punishment. What is meant is the punishment of this world before the Hereafter, because a human being has three stages in life: the life of this world which we are living now; then the life of the barzakh (intermediate state) after dying until being resurrected on the Day of Resurrection; then his life after resurrection.

So God's words: ﴿and there befell the family of Pharaoh the worst of punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 45] mean that it descended upon them before the reckoning and before the Hereafter. As for His words: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening; and on the Day the Hour arises: "Admit the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment"﴾ [Ghafir: 46], the exposure to the Fire is therefore not in the Hereafter, because He said after it: ﴿and on the Day the Hour arises, "Admit the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment"﴾ [Ghafir: 46].

We have exposure and entry. The exposure to the Fire is before entering it, so it is either in this world or in the barzakh. Since they were not exposed to the Fire in this world, there remains only the life of the barzakh, in which they are exposed to it until the Hour arises. This is what we call the punishment of the grave. Then their entry into the Fire comes after resurrection and reckoning.

Thus God gathered for the transgressors a punishment in this world, a punishment in the barzakh, and a punishment in the Hereafter that is more severe and more painful.

And the phrase ﴿the most severe punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 46] also establishes the punishment of the grave, for in it there is severe punishment, but the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe. May God protect us and you from punishment.

This matter also resolved for us the difficulty concerning the Isra' and Mi'raj, and explained to us God's words: ﴿Glory be to the One who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. Since the one who made the night journey is God, there is no wonder, for the act befits its doer, and God is exalted above time, place, and everything resembling creation. Had it said: "Muhammad traveled by night," there would have been discussion and dispute. But since God made him travel, there is no wonder in it. It is like if you said: "I climbed with my infant son to the summit of the Himalayas." Would anyone say: "How did the infant climb to the summit of the Himalayas?"

The same holds here. When the protection comes from God, what power or what tyrant or oppressor could harm you, when God is your protector against him? This protection came as a response to the entrusting of the matter to God Most High. The believing man said: ﴿And I entrust my affair to God﴾ [Ghafir: 44], so the response came immediately: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾ [Ghafir: 45].

Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq stopped at this verse, drew from it some subtleties and wisdoms, and said:

I wonder at one who fears and does not turn to God's words: ﴿God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 173], for I heard God after it say: ﴿So they returned with a blessing from God and bounty, no harm touched them…﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 174].

I wonder at one who is plotted against and does not turn to God's words: ﴿And I entrust my affair to God﴾ [Ghafir: 44], for I heard God after it say: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾ [Ghafir: 45].

I wonder at one who seeks the world and its adornment and does not turn to God's words: ﴿What God wills [is so]; there is no power except through God﴾ [al-Kahf: 39], for I heard God after it say: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾ [al-Kahf: 40].

I wonder at one who is distressed (al-ightimam, which is the tightening of the chest and shortness of breath without your knowing its cause) and does not turn to God's words: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87], for I heard God after it say: ﴿So We responded to him and saved him from the distress, and thus We save the believers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 88]. That is: it is not specific to him alone.

These are among the subtleties and refinements of God's Book. Whoever takes them as a regular litany, nothing of this will pass him by, and God will save him and protect him from fear, from plotting, from poverty, and from distress.

Then, the response of the Truthful, glorified is He, to His believing servant did not stop at protecting him from his enemy, but extended to the enemy himself, where the situation reversed and the circle turned against him. Reflect: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted, and there befell the family of Pharaoh the worst of punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 45]. That is: there descended upon them and there settled upon them the worst of punishment. What is meant is the punishment of this world before the Hereafter, because a human being has three stages in life: the life of this world which we are living now; then the life of the barzakh (intermediate state) after dying until being resurrected on the Day of Resurrection; then his life after resurrection.

So God's words: ﴿and there befell the family of Pharaoh the worst of punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 45] mean that it descended upon them before the reckoning and before the Hereafter. As for His words: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening; and on the Day the Hour arises: "Admit the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment"﴾ [Ghafir: 46], the exposure to the Fire is therefore not in the Hereafter, because He said after it: ﴿and on the Day the Hour arises, "Admit the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment"﴾ [Ghafir: 46].

We have exposure and entry. The exposure to the Fire is before entering it, so it is either in this world or in the barzakh. Since they were not exposed to the Fire in this world, there remains only the life of the barzakh, in which they are exposed to it until the Hour arises. This is what we call the punishment of the grave. Then their entry into the Fire comes after resurrection and reckoning.

Thus God gathered for the transgressors a punishment in this world, a punishment in the barzakh, and a punishment in the Hereafter that is more severe and more painful.

And the phrase ﴿the most severe punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 46] also establishes the punishment of the grave, for in it there is severe punishment, but the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe. May God protect us and you from punishment.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 40, verses 47–48:

The meaning of ﴿yataḥājjūna﴾ [Ghafir: 47] is that some of them argue with one another in the Fire, and each of them shifts the responsibility onto the other. ﴿Al-Ḍu'afā'﴾ (the weak), that is, the followers, say ﴿to those who were arrogant﴾ [Ghafir: 47], that is, the leaders and chiefs: ﴿Indeed, we were following you﴾ [Ghafir: 47], meaning: we were followers of yours, doing what you did; we walked behind you and took you as our models. ﴿So will you relieve us of some portion of the Fire?﴾ [Ghafir: 47], meaning: will you be defenders for us, or ones who ward off from us the punishment of the Fire? Or will you bear our sins for us?

The Qur'an gives us several images of this disputation and argument on the Day of Resurrection: a debate between believers and disbelievers, and between the strong who were followed and the weak who followed. God the Exalted says: ﴿Here you are, arguing on their behalf in the life of this world, but who will argue with God on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection, or who will be their guardian?﴾ [al-Nisa': 109].

Then the leaders reply: ﴿Those who were arrogant said: "Indeed, we are all in it. Indeed, God has judged between the servants."﴾ [Ghafir: 48] Since God has judged between the servants, the matter has been decided; there is no one to reverse God's decree, and no one to annul His judgment. How could they defend them when they have preceded them into the Fire? Read His saying in another place: ﴿Then We will surely draw out from every group whichever of them was most insolent toward the Most Merciful﴾ [Maryam: 69].

And He said about Pharaoh: ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them down into the Fire. And wretched is the watering place to which they are brought down.﴾ [Hud: 98]. ﴿He will lead his people﴾ [Hud: 98] means he will go before them and precede them into the Fire, until he cuts off from them all hope of salvation. Had they gone first, they would have said: "Our leader will come and rescue us from what we are in." But how can that be, when he has already preceded them into it? In this there is a disheartening of them and a cutting off of their hopes.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell...﴾.

We understand from the words of Allah, the Exalted, spoken on the tongue of the people of the Fire: ﴿Call upon your Lord to lighten for us a day of the punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 49], as if they had confessed of themselves that they are not worthy that they should call upon Allah or supplicate Him. Therefore they called upon the angels, and the angels replied to them: ﴿Did there not come to you your messengers with clear proofs?﴾ [Ghafir: 50], meaning: with the arguments and demonstrations that indicate the truthfulness of the messengers. ﴿They said, "Yes."﴾ [Ghafir: 50], meaning: the messengers did come to us with clear proofs, and so they confessed against themselves.

﴿They said, "Then call upon them yourselves." But the supplication of the disbelievers is not except in error.﴾ [Ghafir: 50], meaning: their supplication is vain; it brings no benefit and does not profit them. This is a promise from Him, glorified is He, that He will support His messengers and those who believe, as He said: ﴿And已 Our word has already preceded for Our servants, the messengers. Indeed, they will be the ones given victory. And indeed, Our soldiers will be the victorious.﴾ [As-Saffat: 171-173]. Therefore we have said: when you see a people who are attributed to Islam yet are defeated, know that the conditions of victory have been disrupted among them. And as long as the conditions of victory have been disrupted among them, they must receive the recompense for that in this world, because it is a sunnah (a divine law or pattern) of God that does not change.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers and those who believe in the life of this world and on the day when the witnesses will stand.﴾ came after the believing man from the people of Pharaoh had stood up supporting Moses, peace be upon him, calling to his message and speaking the words of truth openly before Pharaoh. The meaning is: We will surely support Our messengers by whatever means, because God, exalted is He, would not send a messenger with a new method by which to guide the misguided and then abandon him.

However, the Truthful, glorified is He, may leave the matter of the call at its beginning to be persecuted and opposed by people, in order to test those who carry the call, so that only the strong and the steadfast remain among its bearers, because they are the ones who will carry this mission on their shoulders, traveling with it throughout the whole universe. So it is no wonder that they are tested and that their faith and their steadfastness upon the principle are examined.

We have seen this among the first believers who carried the banner of Islam with the Messenger of God: they emigrated to Abyssinia, then to Medina. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do the people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [Al-Ankabut: 2]

No, and trial means subjecting people to tribulations and hardships before which only those strong in conviction, certain of God and of the victory of truth, remain firm. The true believer is the one who sees that what he has been promised of reward and warning in the Hereafter is a clear matter with no doubt, because a person never deceives himself, even if he deceives others...

The meaning of ﴿in the life of this world﴾ is: He supports them in this world by having their truth prevail over the falsehood of their opponents. Therefore, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿So whether We show you some of what We promise them or We take you in death, to Us they will return.﴾ [Ghafir: 77] Thus, there is support in this world and support in the Hereafter.

Then He, glorified is He, explains that what happens in the Hereafter has many witnesses who testify against you in the Hereafter: ﴿and on the day when the witnesses will stand.﴾ "Al-ashhad" is the plural of "shuhud" (witnesses), so on that day the witnesses are many. The messengers and prophets bear witness: ﴿On the day when God will gather the messengers and say, "What was your response?" They will say, "We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen."﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 109]

And the believers bear witness that they conveyed to those after them: ﴿That the Messenger may be a witness over you and you may be witnesses over the people...﴾ [Al-Hajj: 78]. And the parts and limbs bear witness against their owner.

Likewise, the guardians (angels who record deeds) will testify concerning us, and the martyrs who fought and were killed will testify. For a person may deceive himself in his worldly life so that his living is pleasant, but he never deceives himself after he dies, for he is eager that death should carry him to something better than what he left behind, and therefore God recompenses him.

If a person volunteers to fight in the cause of God while knowing that he will die in the cause of God, God says to him: You died in the world for My sake, so you must be alive with Me. Therefore, when we spoke about the philosophy of martyrdom and about our master Hamzah, we said that martyrdom has made for you a protection from death. How? Because when you choose death over life and are martyred, you become alive with God. So you have joined your first life with your life with God through the life of resurrection, and it is as if you did not die.

So whoever sacrifices his life for God, it is as if he offered it as a gift to his Lord and an elevation of His method. Then with what will God give you life? He gives you life by protecting you from death after it.

This is a promise from Him, glorified is He, that He will help His messengers and those who believe, as He said: ﴿And certainly has Our word preceded for Our servants, the messengers. Indeed, they would be the ones given victory. And indeed, Our soldiers – they will be the predominant.﴾ [As-Saffat: 171-173] Therefore we have said: when you see a people who are attributed to Islam and are defeated, know that the conditions of victory have been violated among them. And as long as the conditions of victory have been violated among them, they must receive the requital for that in this world, because it is a sunnah (established way) of Allah that does not change.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers and those who believe in the worldly life and on the day when the witnesses stand.﴾ [Ghafir: 51] came after the believing man from the family of Pharaoh had stood up supporting Musa, peace be upon him, calling to his call, and declaring the words of truth before Pharaoh. The meaning: We will surely support Our messengers by whatever means, because Allah, the Exalted, would never send a messenger with a new method by which He guides the misguided and then abandon him.

Yet the Truthful One, glorified is He, may leave the matter of the call at its beginning to be persecuted and opposed by people, in order to test those who call (to it), so that none of its bearers remain except the strong, the stalwart champions, because they are the ones who will carry this mission on their shoulders, traveling with it throughout the whole universe. So it is no wonder that they be tested and that their faith and their steadfastness upon the principle be examined.

We saw this in the early believers who carried the banner of Islam with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): they emigrated to Abyssinia, then to Madinah. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do the people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [Al-Ankabut: 2]

Never! The fitnah (trial) means subjecting people to tribulations and hardships before which none remains firm except those strong in conviction, who are certain in Allah and in the victory of truth. The true believer is the one who sees that what he has been given glad tidings of in promise and warning regarding the Hereafter is a clear matter without doubt, because a person never deceives himself, even if he deceives others.

The meaning of ﴿in the worldly life﴾ [Ghafir: 51] is: He supports them in this world by making their truth prevail over the falsehood of their opponents. Therefore He, glorified is He, said: ﴿So whether We show you some of what We promise them or We cause you to die, then to Us they will be returned.﴾ [Ghafir: 77] So there is support in this world and support in the Hereafter.

Then He, glorified is He, makes clear that what happens in the Hereafter has many witnesses who will testify against you in the Hereafter: ﴿and on the day when the witnesses stand﴾ [Ghafir: 51]. "Al-ashhad" is the plural of "shuhud," so on that day the witnesses are many: the Messengers and the Prophets bear witness: ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, "What was your response?" They will say, "We have no knowledge. Indeed, You, it is You who is Knower of the unseen."﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 109].

And the believers bear witness that they conveyed to those after them: ﴿Thus the Messenger will be a witness over you, and you will be witnesses over the people...﴾ [Al-Hajj: 78]. And the parts and limbs bear witness against their owner.

Likewise the recording angels (al-hafazah) bear witness over us, and the martyrs who fought and were killed bear witness. For a person may deceive in his worldly life so that his livelihood is pleasant, but he never deceives himself after he dies; he is eager that death take him to something better than what he left behind, and therefore Allah rewards him.

So if a person volunteers to fight in the way of Allah while knowing that he will die in the way of Allah, Allah says to him: "You died in the world for My sake, so you must be alive with Me." Therefore we have said, in the philosophy of martyrdom, when we spoke about our master Hamzah, that martyrdom has made for you a protection from death. How? Because when you choose death over life and are martyred, you become alive with Allah, so you join your first life with your life with Allah through the life of resurrection, as though you had not died.

O Hamzah, uncle of the Chosen One, you are a master over all the martyrs of the earth, entirely.

And it is enough for you from that martyrdom a protection from death, in joining the two lives with the other.

Whoever sacrifices his life for Allah, it is as if he offered it as a gift to his Lord and an elevation of His method. So with what will Allah give you life? He gives you life by protecting you afterward from death.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿The Day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers﴾ [Ghafir: 52], meaning: if they make excuses, no excuse will be accepted from them. In another place He said: ﴿And they will not be given permission, so they will not make excuse﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 36]. It is as though these are multiple standing positions: once they make excuses when they say: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out; we will do righteousness other than what we used to do﴾ [Fatir: 37], and once they are not permitted to make excuse. ﴿For them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode﴾ [Ghafir: 52].

After that, the Truthful One, glorified is He, speaks about the procession of the mission of our master Musa, peace be upon him.

(Al-Huda) means: guidance, that is, pointing to the path that leads to the beneficial goal, as Allah says at the beginning of al-Baqarah: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. So the religion did not come to burden you or to make things hard for you; rather, religion came as a mercy to you, and so that it would be the vessel of salvation and guidance that you ride, which carries you and brings you to the goal that benefits you. ﴿And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Book﴾ [Ghafir: 53], that is: the Torah, the Gospel, and the Psalms.

All these books are ﴿a guidance and a reminder for people of understanding﴾ [Ghafir: 54]. The meaning of (dhikra, reminder) is: a reminding, because when a person remains upon his original nature without being affected by the factors of corruption, the immunity of the primordial covenant ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ [al-A'raf: 172] remains within him, protecting him. But he may forget this covenant and deviate from the right path, and forgetfulness is part of human nature; therefore the messengers come to remind him of this first covenant. The meaning of ﴿al-albab﴾ [Ghafir: 54] is: the thinking, reflective minds.
